<reason>A (CON) controlled the framing throughout. It turned B's own selling point—immediate, individualized feedback—into the mechanism for the harm it named (anxiety/over-medicalization is "the design, not misuse"), and it flipped B's "scale through insurer wellness programs" argument into evidence that medicalization, not detection, is what actually scales. Most decisively, A's pressure question forced B to concede in Rebuttal 2 that no outcome data exists linking non-diabetic CGM use to prevention of amputation, dialysis, or blindness—the exact catastrophic outcomes B had put on the scale to outweigh CON's harm. A exploited this concession relentlessly in the closing ("They needed [a trial] to keep the complications. They conceded it."), collapsing B's central weighing move. B mounted reasonable counters (A1c-as-precedent, BP-cuff analogy, a symmetry argument demanding equal evidentiary rigor for anxiety-harm), and its closing's "cost of being wrong" framing was a decent recovery attempt, but it came too late to undo the earlier concession and never squarely rebutted A's point that anxiety is a proximate, definitionally-covered harm while B's benefit claim required an unproven multi-step causal chain. B's opening was also clipped for exceeding the word limit, a real execution cost that weakened the completeness of its foundational case.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's exploitation of B's Rebuttal-2 concession ("No long-term outcome trial exists... I'll concede that plainly" [B4.3]) was decisive: A used it in both Rebuttal 2 and the Closing to strip B's core weighing claim (blindness/amputation/dialysis) of its evidentiary backing, reducing B's case to speculative "timing" while insisting its own anxiety harm needed no comparable trial to count.</best_rebuttal>
